recent_posts.title: Hedged DRAM reads to eliminate memory refresh tail latency
recent_posts.summary: DRAM refresh cycles (TRFC) cause periodic memory stalls every ~3.9 microseconds, adding up to 400-500ns of latency when a read coincides with a refresh. This deep-dive explores a novel technique called 'Tail Slayer' that reduces P99.99 tail latency by 7-15x. The approach uses hedged reads: duplicating data across independent memory channels so two threads on separate cores race to read the same data, and whichever avoids the refresh stall wins. Key challenges covered include virtual vs physical memory addressing, huge pages, reverse-engineering undocumented CPU memory controller XOR hash functions (for AMD Zen4/5, Intel Sapphire/Granite Rapids, and AWS Graviton ARM) using hardware performance counters and statistical timing analysis. Benchmarks on bare-metal cloud instances confirm dramatic tail latency improvements across DDR4/DDR5, x86, and ARM architectures. The technique is particularly relevant for high-frequency trading systems where a single DRAM stall can cost millions.

recent_posts.title: Five computer science predictions for 2026
recent_posts.summary: A set of five technical predictions for 2026 covering: (1) CXL-backed tiered memory becoming a cloud offering as RAM prices rise and the Linux kernel matures its memory tiering support; (2) a coordinated lunar time standard being officially published, driven by general relativity making moon-time drift from Earth-time; (3) CHERI (Cherry) capability-based hardware memory safety gaining traction as a hardware-level alternative to rewriting codebases in Rust; (4) a major package repository like npm being forced to shut down registrations due to AI-assisted supply chain attacks and 'slop squatting'; and (5) LLVM adding a third ML-guided optimization heuristic, making compiler output non-deterministic at maximum optimization levels.

recent_posts.title: Notable computer science research papers from 2025
recent_posts.summary: A roundup of notable computer science research from 2025 includes an undergraduate student accidentally discovering a hash table optimization that beats a Turing Award winner's solution, Valve's gaming-focused CPU scheduler being adopted by Meta for data centers, researchers using a dog to replicate IBM's quantum factorization records to critique overhyped quantum computing claims, CXL fork technology enabling process snapshots across clusters for faster scaling, and a new algorithm that mathematically beats Dijkstra's shortest path algorithm though practical benefits require billions of nodes.

recent_posts.title: How fighter jets use restricted C++ for safety critical systems
recent_posts.summary: Explores the Joint Strike Fighter (JSF) C++ coding standard used in F-35 development, demonstrating how safety-critical aerospace software achieves reliability by surgically removing language features like exceptions, recursion, and dynamic memory allocation. The piece traces the evolution from Ada to C++ in military aviation, explains key restrictions through live flight simulator demonstrations, and connects these principles to modern standards like NASA's F-Prime and automotive AutoSAR.

recent_posts.title: Programming Isn't Math, It's Linguistics
recent_posts.summary: Programming languages face similar ambiguity challenges as human languages. The content explores how compilers parse code through three phases (lexical analysis, parsing, and semantic analysis) and demonstrates common C++ syntax ambiguities like the "most vexing parse," dangling else problem, nested generics parsing, and dependent type names. These issues arise because compilers must interpret code without context, similar to how written language can be ambiguous without tone or punctuation cues. The piece includes practical examples showing how modern C++ standards have resolved many historical parsing problems.

recent_posts.title: Self replicating compiler backdoors and Thompson's trusting trust attack
recent_posts.summary: Ken Thompson's 1984 Turing Award speech introduced a terrifying concept: self-replicating compiler backdoors that persist across generations. The attack exploits self-hosted compilers (compilers written in the language they compile) to inject malicious code that reproduces itself in subsequent compiler versions, making detection nearly impossible even with complete source code audits. The piece demonstrates this through quine programs and obfuscation techniques, explains how LLVM's widespread use could amplify such attacks across multiple languages, and discusses mitigation strategies like diverse double-compiling. The XcodeGhost malware incident proves this theoretical attack has real-world precedent, and Thompson himself admitted to implementing a version at Bell Labs.

recent_posts.title: What happens when humanity loses CPU manufacturing ability
recent_posts.summary: A thought experiment exploring what would happen if humanity lost the ability to manufacture CPUs. The scenario traces the gradual decline of modern computing over 30 years, from cloud infrastructure failures to internet fragmentation, highlighting how older hardware with larger node sizes would outlast modern chips due to electromigration. The piece examines how software optimization would become critical, vintage computing would resurge, and society would eventually revert to 1970s-80s era technology.

recent_posts.title: Reverse engineering obfuscated C code contest submissions with Ghidra
recent_posts.summary: A reverse engineer analyzes obfuscated C code submissions from the International Obfuscated C Code Contest (IOCCC) using Ghidra decompiler. The analysis reveals surprising implementations including a Rick Roll animation, a complete Doom game running in a virtual machine, a 3D renderer, an LLM chatbot with multiple personalities, a Vim clone, and other creative programs. The experiment demonstrates both the effectiveness of reverse engineering tools and the ingenuity of obfuscated code techniques.

recent_posts.title: How iOS hides its complex file system behind simple interfaces
recent_posts.summary: iOS devices have a sophisticated Unix-based file system with hierarchical directory structure, despite Apple's decade-long effort to hide it from users. The system uses APFS (Apple File System) and heavily relies on SQLite databases for data storage. Apple originally removed file management from the iPhone in 2007 to simplify user experience, but reintroduced the Files app in iOS 11 due to limitations with the iPad Pro. The Files app itself creates an illusion of direct file access while actually using SQLite lookups to maintain app sandboxing and security.
